blocks.c: 29. The Last Two Pages
Page ten is definitions.

Page eleven is the execution block: a signature line for the landlord, which has never been signed by anything, and a signature line for the caretaker, which has been signed eleven times, and each signature is smaller and shakier than the one above it, and the last one is Wen's, from October 1994, and it is a firm confident twenty-four-year-old's signature and it made me want to put my fist through something.
Page ten is where they buried it.
"Occupation" means the presence within the premises of a Caretaker who maintains the Record.
"The Record" means the current maintenance log of the premises.
"Current" means the volume in use at the material time.
I read it three times.
"Wen. What's the current maintenance log?"
"The black one. This year's. It's in your bag."
"Right. And what's this?" I held up the blue one. 1994.
"That's mine. That's not current, it's—"
She stopped.
We looked at each other in the light of a dying head torch on the landing of a floor that does not exist.
"It says the volume in use at the material time," I said. "Not the volume issued for the current year. In use."
"That is the most lawyer thing I have ever—"
"Wen. Have you been writing in the 1994 book for thirty-one years?"
"Every single day," said Wen Aguilar.

"Then it's in use," I said. "Then there are two current maintenance logs in this building, and two people maintaining them, and the definition doesn't say a caretaker maintains the Record, it says a Caretaker who maintains the Record, and there is no article anywhere in this document that says there can only be one of us."
Somewhere below us, in a warehouse full of boxes, a photocopier started up.
